drivingQuestion: Do the dead know what the living do around them, given the verse 'and the dead know nothing'?
outcomeNote: R' Yonatan's objection is answered by re-reading Ecclesiastes 9:5 of the wicked; the difficulty against the alternative prooftext is likewise answered, and the two readings of the snowy-day clause are left standing side by side without decision.

segments.he: רַבִּי חִיָּיא וְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן הֲווֹ שָׁקְלִי וְאָזְלִי בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת. הֲוָה קָשַׁדְיָא תְּכֵלְתָּא דְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן. אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא: דַּלְיַיהּ, כְּדַי שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ: לְמָחָר בָּאִין אֶצְלֵנוּ, וְעַכְשָׁיו מְחָרְפִין אוֹתָנוּ.
segments.en: The Gemara relates that «Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery and the sky-blue string» of «Rabbi Yonatan’s» ritual fringes «was cast» to the ground and dragging across the graves. «Rabbi Ḥiyya said» to him: «Lift it, so» the dead «will not say: Tomorrow,» when their day comes, they will «come to» be buried with «us, and now» they are «insulting us.»

segments.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּמִי יָדְעִי כּוּלֵּי הַאי? וְהָא כְּתִיב: ״וְהַמֵּתִים אֵינָם יוֹדְעִים מְאוּמָה״! אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם קָרִיתָ — לֹא שָׁנִיתָ. אִם שָׁנִיתָ — לֹא שִׁלַּשְׁתָּ. אִם שִׁלַּשְׁתָּ — לֹא פֵּירְשׁוּ לְךָ. ״כִּי הַחַיִּים יוֹדְעִים שֶׁיָּמוּתוּ״ — אֵלּוּ צַדִּיקִים שֶׁבְּמִיתָתָן נִקְרְאוּ חַיִּים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וּבְנָיָהוּ בֶן יְהוֹיָדָע בֶּן אִישׁ חַי רַב פְּעָלִים מִקַּבְצְאֵל הוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִאֵל מוֹאָב וְהוּא יָרַד וְהִכָּה אֶת הָאֲרִי בְּתוֹךְ הַבּוֹר בְּיוֹם הַשָּׁלֶג״.
segments.en: Rabbi Yonatan «said to him: Do» the dead «know so much? Isn’t it stated: “And the dead know nothing”» (Ecclesiastes 9:5)? Rabbi Ḥiyya «said to him: If you read» the verse, «you did not» read it «a second time, and if you» read it «a second time, you did not» read it «a third time, and if you» read it «a third time, they did not explain it to you» properly. The meaning of the verse: “For the living know that they will die, and the dead know nothing and have no more reward, for their memory has been forgotten” (Ecclesiastes 9:5): «For the living know that they will die, these are the righteous, who even in their death are called living.» An allusion to this is «as it is stated: “And Benayahu, son of Yehoyada, son of a valiant man of Kabze’el, who had done mighty deeds, he smote the two altar-hearths of Moab; he went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow”» (II Samuel 23:20).

segments.he: ״בֶּן אִישׁ חַי״: אַטּוּ כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא בְּנֵי מֵתֵי נִינְהוּ? אֶלָּא: ״בֶּן אִישׁ חַי״ — שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בְּמִיתָתוֹ קָרוּי חַי. ״רַב פְּעָלִים מִקַּבְצְאֵל״ — שֶׁרִיבָּה וְקִבֵּץ פּוֹעֲלִים לַתּוֹרָה. ״וְהוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִאֵל מוֹאָב״ — שֶׁלֹּא הִנִּיחַ כְּמוֹתוֹ לֹא בְּמִקְדָּשׁ רִאשׁוֹן וְלֹא בְּמִקְדָּשׁ שֵׁנִי.
segments.en: He was referred to in the verse as «son of a living man.» The Gemara wonders: «Is that to say,» the fact that the Bible referred to him with that appellation, «that all others are children of the dead? Rather,» the verse should be explained as follows: «The son of a living man» who lives forever, «who even in death is referred to as living. Man of Kabze’el who had done mighty deeds, as he accumulated and gathered many workers for» the sake of the «Torah. Who killed the two lion-hearted men [Ariel] of Moab, as» after his death «he left no one his equal, in either the First Temple or the Second Temple» periods, as the Temple is called Ariel (see Isaiah 29:1), and the two Ariel refers to the two Temples.

segments.he: ״וְהוּא יָרַד וְהִכָּה אֶת הָאֲרִי בְּתוֹךְ הַבּוֹר בְּיוֹם הַשָּׁלֶג״, אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: דְּתַבַּר גְּזִיזֵי דְבַרְדָּא, וּנְחַת וּטְבַל. אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: דִּתְנָא סִיפְרָא דְבֵי רַב בְּיוֹמָא דְסִיתְוָא.
segments.en: The Sages disagreed over the interpretation of the rest of the verse: «“And who descended and slew the lion in the pit on the snowy day.” Some say» that this means «that he broke blocks of hail and descended and immersed himself» in the water to purify himself. «Others say that he learned» all of «the Sifra,» the halakhic midrash on the book of Leviticus «of the school of Rav,» on a «winter’s day.»

segments.he: ״וְהַמֵּתִים אֵינָם יוֹדְעִים מְאוּמָה״ — אֵלּוּ רְשָׁעִים, שֶׁבְּחַיֵּיהֶן קְרוּיִין ״מֵתִים״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְאַתָּה חָלָל רָשָׁע נְשִׂיא יִשְׂרָאֵל״. וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא, מֵהָכָא: ״עַל פִּי שְׁנַיִם עֵדִים אוֹ עַל פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה עֵדִים יוּמַת הַמֵּת״, חַי הוּא! אֶלָּא, הַמֵּת מֵעִיקָּרָא.
segments.en: In contrast to the righteous, who are referred to as living even after their death, the verse states explicitly: «“The dead know nothing.” These are the wicked, who» even «during their lives are called dead, as» the prophet Ezekiel «said» in reference to a king of Israel who was alive: «“And you are a slain, wicked prince of Israel”» (Ezekiel 21:30). «And if you wish, say» instead that the proof is «from here: “At the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses the dead shall be put to death”» (Deuteronomy 17:6). This is puzzling. As long as the accused has not been sentenced to death, he «is alive. Rather,» this person who is wicked is considered «dead from the outset.»

moves.cueHe: רבי חייא ורבי יונתן הוו שקלי ואזלי בבית הקברות
moves.summary: The two sages walk in a cemetery and R' Yonatan's sky-blue fringe drags over the graves.
moves.about: the two were walking together in a cemetery when R' Yonatan's sky-blue fringe dragged over the graves

moves.summary: R' Ḥiyya tells him to lift it, lest the dead say the living insult them today and join them tomorrow.
moves.about: instructing him to lift the dragging fringe so the dead will not be insulted

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה: ומי ידעי כולי האי? והא כתיב
moves.summary: R' Yonatan objects from 'and the dead know nothing' that the dead have no such awareness.
moves.about: whether the dead have any awareness at all, given a verse that says they know nothing

moves.cueHe: אמר ליה: אם קרית — לא שנית
moves.summary: R' Ḥiyya answers that the verse was never properly expounded to him.
moves.about: the verse R' Yonatan quoted has never been properly expounded to him and does not mean what he assumes

moves.summary: The verse's 'living' are the righteous, who are called living even in death.
moves.about: the inadequacy of R' Yonatan's study of the verse he cited

moves.cueHe: שנאמר: ״ובניהו בן יהוידע בן איש חי״
moves.summary: Benayahu, 'son of a living man', is brought as the allusion.
moves.about: 'the living know that they will die' refers to the righteous, who are called living even in their death

moves.cueHe: ״בן איש חי״: אטו כולי עלמא בני מתי נינהו?
moves.summary: If the phrase is literal, are all other men sons of the dead?
moves.about: why the verse singles Benayahu out as 'son of a living man' — everyone else is not a son of the dead

moves.cueHe: אלא: ״בן איש חי״ — שאפילו במיתתו קרוי חי
moves.summary: The phrase means one who is called living even in his death.
moves.about: 'son of a living man' means one who is called living even in his death, not a contrast with other people's fathers

moves.cueHe: ״רב פעלים מקבצאל״ — שריבה וקבץ פועלים לתורה
moves.summary: The next phrase of the verse is expounded: he gathered many workers for Torah.
moves.about: 'of many deeds, from Kabze'el' means he multiplied and gathered workers for Torah

moves.cueHe: ״והוא הכה את שני אראל מואב״ — שלא הניח כמותו
moves.summary: 'The two ariel of Moav' — he left no equal in either Temple.
moves.about: 'he smote the two ariel of Moav' means he left no equal to himself in either the First or the Second Temple

moves.cueHe: ״והוא ירד והכה את הארי בתוך הבור ביום השלג״, איכא דאמרי
moves.summary: First anonymous reading: he broke blocks of ice, descended and immersed.
moves.about: 'he went down and smote the lion in the pit on a snowy day' means he broke blocks of ice and immersed himself

moves.cueHe: איכא דאמרי: דתנא סיפרא דבי רב ביומא דסיתוא
moves.summary: Second anonymous reading: he learned the whole Sifra of the school of Rav in one winter day.
moves.about: the snowy-day clause means he studied the whole Sifra of the school of Rav in one winter day

moves.summary: The second half of the verse is expounded of the wicked, who are called dead in their lifetime — which removes R' Yonatan's objection.
moves.about: 'and the dead know nothing' speaks of the wicked, who are called dead even while alive — so it does not deny awareness to the righteous dead

moves.summary: Ezekiel calls a living wicked prince 'slain'.
moves.about: a living wicked king addressed by the prophet as 'slain', proving the wicked are called dead while alive

moves.summary: An alternative prooftext is offered: 'the dead shall be put to death'.
moves.about: an alternative prooftext: 'the dead shall be put to death' calls the condemned man dead while he is still alive

moves.summary: He is 'the dead' from the outset because he is wicked — which is precisely the proof.
moves.about: supporting the claim that the wicked are called dead in their lifetime with a second, alternative prooftext

moves.summary: But the condemned man is still alive when the verse calls him dead.
moves.about: the alternative prooftext seems unusable: the condemned man is still alive when the verse calls him 'the dead'
